implementation_notes: C# makes publish-subscribe a language feature: the event keyword exposes add/remove accessors over a multicast delegate (typically EventHandler<T>), += and -= are subscribe and unsubscribe, and ?.Invoke raises the event to every registered handler synchronously, so no registry is hand-written. Multi-subscriber fan-out is simply the delegate invocation list. Events are in-process only; cross-process broadcast needs a broker (Service Bus topics, RabbitMQ fanout).
pitfalls: A handler that throws aborts the loop over the invocation list, so later subscribers never see the event; isolate handler failures.
Events hold strong references to their subscribers: a discarded subscriber that forgot -= keeps the publisher and its object graph alive.
Only the declaring class may raise the event; derived classes cannot invoke a base event directly and need a protected virtual raiser.

variants.name: System.Reactive IObservable/Subject
variants.implementation_notes: Rx.NET turns the channel into an observable stream: Subject<T> is the publisher that fans out to every subscribed IObserver<T>, and Subscribe returns an IDisposable that is the unsubscribe token. Choose it over plain events when subscribers need operators (filter, throttle, buffer, composition) and explicit disposable lifetimes; the cost is a NuGet dependency and a second abstraction (IObservable) in the call path.
pitfalls: Rx subscriptions are only torn down by disposing their IDisposable; dropping the token leaks the observer exactly like an unsubscribed event handler.
OnError/OnCompleted are terminal: after either signal the subject is finished, and subscribers that expected plain fan-out silently stop receiving.
Subject<T> is not thread-safe for concurrent OnNext calls; use serialized subjects (or synchronization) when publishers are parallel.
